title: Sequencing Grants
text:
We will be giving many awards in the amount of ~$5,200 USD to support short-read, whole genome Illumina sequencing of your samples to ~8x coverage. We have competitive pricing from Harvard Bauer Core (Boston, USA) for sequencing.
Investigators will send their extracted DNA on standard SPS plates (96 well or 384 well) directly to Harvard Bauer Core. The pricing is better for samples organized on 384 well plates. As a ballpark estimate, the cost for whole genome sequencing of 60 samples of a 1Gb genome to at least 8x coverage is about $5200. Investigators who wish to sequence more samples or to higher coverage are welcome to do so through a cost-sharing mechanism.
Applicants who are interested in sequencing more than one species should independent applications for each species.

title: Sequencing Grants
text:
Prepare to apply

Before you apply, please join MacroMar as a member.
Before you apply, please obtain a MacroMar ID for your dataset by filling out the Intent to Contribute a Dataset Form for each species.
We expect that you are prepared to submit your samples for whole genome sequencing within 3 months of submitting your application. When you apply, tissue samples should be in hand and the application will ask for the status of DNA extraction.
In the application you will be asked to submit sample metadata in our standardized spreadsheet format. Download the metadata template here.
If you will be shipping extracted DNA from overseas, you are responsible for the applicable permits. More information can be found here. Most biological materials will not need a permit, but protected species do. For example, you must obtain reciprocal CITES permits or certificates from both the exporting and importing countries before shipping extracted DNA from a protected species.
In the application you will be asked to submit a cost estimate in a standardized spreadsheet format. Download the cost estimate spreadsheet here and follow the instructions on the README.

If you would like to request more than $5200 USD from MacroMar, please follow the instructions in the spreadsheet to change the amount covered by MacroMar. Due to the submission system, costs will be covered on a unit basis (e.g., either library prep for X samples, or sequencing only, or some combination of library prep and sequencing). We will consider exceptions for research groups who do not currently have funding or have very large genomes and whose total exceeds $5200 USD for 60 samples to 8x coverage.

The application will ask, if you are awarded, that you agree to follow the MacroMar workflow for bioinformatics and share the resulting VCF files with the MacroMar project via our authorship and data usage policy

title: Sequencing Grants
text:
Scoring rubric
Applications will be scored according to the following rubric:

State of sampling (highest score for samples in hand with extracted DNA)
Metadata submitted with application (highest score for data submitted in our standardized format)
Samples representative of: species range, population structure, and/or environmental gradients (highest score for all three)
Biogeographic representation (highest score for samples from underrepresented habitats or geographic areas)
Reference exists (highest score for publicly available reference)
Taxonomic/Phylogenetic representation (highest score for phyla underrepresented in MacroMar or RepAdapt)
Ability to match funds or statement of financial need

title: Statement of Collaboration and Code of Conduct
text: The MacroMar Network is dedicated to promoting collaboration, networking, and the exchange of knowledge. We welcome and encourage participation by all individuals, at any career stage, who have a genuine interest in participating in the project. We strive to cultivate a network built on encouragement, acceptance, and mutual respect, thereby engendering a welcoming environment for all. We will further promote inclusion by fostering a focus on belonging in membership, leadership, committees, outreach, public engagement, recruitment, and in all other areas of activity within the network. We define inclusion as the process of increasing the presence, participation, and achievement of all network members, while attending to the diversity of nationalities, career stages, and identities represented across the MacroMar community.

title: Statement of Collaboration and Code of Conduct
text:
Expectations of members
Members of this marine seascape genomics network commit to the highest standards of scientific integrity, ethics, and environmental stewardship.   The goal of our project is to conduct and facilitate open science. All products will eventually be made publicly available to the fullest extent possible. We expect members of the network to share these values, while respecting Indigenous controls, other forms of controlled access, data sharing agreements, data embargos, and the contributions of others. Members are expected to follow the FAIR and CARE principles, respect the Nagoya Protocol on Access and Benefit-Sharing, honor the rights of coastal and Indigenous peoples, and promote collaboration. Research conducted in developing nations or localized territories must actively involve, empower, and resource scientists from those regions. The network enforces a zero-tolerance policy for harassment, discrimination, bullying, or exploitation in the field, the laboratory, and digital workspaces.
Members are prohibited from sharing embargoed, restricted, or controlled data with chatbots or other AI tools that may retain, use, or further distribute the information.
For authorship and reporting guidelines we will refer participants to the Vancouver Recommendations: a set of recommendations for best practice and ethical standards in the conduct and reporting of published research. They recommend that all 4 of the following criteria are required for authorship: (i) Substantial contributions to the conception or design of the work; or the acquisition, analysis, or interpretation of data for the work; AND (ii) drafting the work or revising it critically for important intellectual content; AND (iii) final approval of the version to be published; AND (iv) agreement to be accountable for all aspects of the work in ensuring that questions related to the accuracy or integrity of any part of the work are appropriately investigated and resolved.
We expect members of the network and its working groups to negotiate authorship structures at the onset of a project, with clear agreements on expectations and roles for all authors that include plans if those expectations are not met. We expect authorship should be offered to local collaborators, technicians, and early-career researchers who contribute significantly to the project’s viability.
Members who contribute data to or conduct large-scale syntheses will agree to our Data Sharing and Authorship Agreement, which will outline authorship policies specific to the use of datasets before and after publication, and will mandate eventual data archiving on a public repository except in clearly-defined special cases. We expect that members who request access to the datasets before they are publicly available for synthesis projects will show a history of engagement with the network.

title: Statement of Collaboration and Code of Conduct
text:
Special cases
We ask that our members recognize that we live in a unique time, with strong political forces that can potentially dictate who is allowed to participate in this project. We recognize that some participants, or potential participants, may face hurdles in whether they are allowed to collaborate internationally or use specific scientific terms, with serious consequences that could cause them to lose their livelihood. We ask that members practice patience and understanding as we navigate a shifting political landscape, and strive to develop an inclusive environment.
In addition, some data may not be suited for public use, such as the specific geographic locations of rare or endangered species, or data that Indigenous people have authority to control. Our network will develop recommendations for such cases and help researchers follow best practices. We intend for data collected and disseminated through this project to be “as open as possible, as closed as necessary”. We are committed to the development of new modes of collaboration, engagement, and partnership with Indigenous Peoples for the care and stewardship of past and future heritage collections. We see public data archiving and data control by Indigenous peoples and local communities as joint priorities that are not at odds, and these twin goals will be reflected in our Data Sharing and Authorship Agreement.

title: Statement of Collaboration and Code of Conduct
text:
Reporting Mechanisms
Violations of this Code of Conduct—including ethical breaches in MacroMar datasets, data misconduct, violation of data sharing agreements or embargoes, failure to recognize individual contributions, or workplace harassment at MacroMar workshops, working groups, or events—should be reported to a member of the MacroMar Investigator Team.
An Ethics Committee will be formed to investigate all formal complaints impartially. Confirmed violations will result in tiered disciplinary actions, which may include: (i) temporary suspension of access to network data repositories and funding channels, and (ii) permanent revocation of membership and notification sent to the member’s home institution compliance officer.

section: An open science ecosystem for enabling macrogenomic research in the sea
text:
An open science ecosystem for enabling macrogenomic research in the sea
Macrogenetics is an emerging field that seeks to combine population genomic datasets across species to study genetic variation and biodiversity.
We are an international network of scientists, students, and researchers working to make data FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable), while following best principles for working with local peoples and rare or endangered species.

section: Our goal is to compile 5,000 whole genomes from 100 species by 2029.
text:
Our goal is to compile 5,000 whole genomes from 100 species by 2029.
These data will serve as a resource for the community to address major unanswered questions in evolutionary biology using marine systems, which host many phyla not found on land yet remain understudied.
We are grateful to the Moore Foundation for funding our network activities

title: Submit Data
text:
The goal of this project is to make seascape genomic data and associated metadata FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable). To maintain interoperability, we require all samples to use short-read sequencing technology, the same bioinformatics pipeline, and the same metadata format.
Seascape genomics is the study of how spatial and environmental factors, such as ocean currents, barriers, and environmental gradients shape the genetic makeup and adaptation of marine species (Riginos et al 2016). Thus, seascape genomic data consists of population genomic data from wild samples, geospatial sampling locations, the date of sampling, and variables that describe the environmental context.

title: Submit Data
text:
Data requirements

Samples collected directly from the wild
Short-read whole genome sequencing (Illumina or AVITI)

High coverage data preferred 8x minimum coverage per individual
Pool-seq data accepted for species with large genomes or that are hard to sample and sequencing individually (like plankton). Recommended 40 individuals per pool with at least 80x coverage per pool for diploids.
For individuals with large genomes (>3Gb), Exome capture data is acceptable
Low-coverage data (<5x coverage per individual) not accepted

Multiple individuals.

For high coverage data: We aim to have at least 50 individuals per species, but datasets of ~100 individuals spanning a phenotypic or environmental gradient, or that are representative of the species range or population structure would be more ideal. We will also accept datasets with fewer individuals, such as for rare or endangered species, or hard-to-obtain samples.
For pool seq data: We recommend at least 40 individuals per pool and 80x coverage per pool, with at least 20 pools.
Please note that we are interested in all species, regardless of whether there is strong population structure or local adaptation.

A reference genome exists
Sufficient metadata for each sample, including the latitude, longitude, depth, and time of sampling.

Ideally, historical environmental data is also available for each sample (one of the goals of this project will be to determine how to summarize this data in a standardized way). Currently we do not have specific requirements for the resolution or minimum time span of historical environmental data, but please be prepared to list sources of relevant environmental data when you submit your samples.

Optional: trait data associated with each sample

title: About MacroMar
text:
The goal of this project is to create enabling conditions for macrogenomic studies in the sea by consolidating a set of interoperable seascape genomic datasets for 5000 whole genomes - each with relevant metadata - representative of 100 marine species by 2029 that meet FAIR and CARE data standards. The outcome will enable large-scale, discovery-driven macrogenomic syntheses and facilitate transformative research on the drivers of genetic diversity and structure in marine populations. Such an endeavor is critical for understanding the oceans because global syntheses in marine systems often reveal different outcomes from terrestrial species that can be counterintuitive. Our project will not only reduce obstacles to macrogenomic research, but will result in coordinated research and educational activities on an international scale with a roadmap for the future.
Through coordinated research activities, we aim to create the conditions for tackling fundamental, long-standing questions and for testing evolutionary theory. Here are some examples of fundamental questions we aim to address with this research:

title: About MacroMar
text:
Aim 1
Our first Aim is to build community, coordinate efforts, and establish standards via Regional Foundation Workshop. To coordinate efforts, we will hold a series of virtual meetings leading up to the in person workshops with key folks from the participating networks. The goal of the workshops will be to form working groups that will tackle key topics, such as but not limited to: Indigenous genomic standards/metadata, data interoperability, marine environmental data, AI-term matching, polyploid data, and population genomics of plankton.

title: About MacroMar
text:
Aim 2
Our second aim focuses on making population genomic data interoperable by running it through the same bioinformatics pipeline and by ensuring associated metadata is in a standardized format. We will support the Local Research Pods and use stipend initiatives to promote the completion of projects and to create opportunities for early career researchers.

title: About MacroMar
text:
Aim 3
Our third aim will be to conduct synthesis of datasets and a horizon scan. A horizon scan identifies developing trends, anticipates risks and opportunities, and develops plans to build resilience against disruptions. We will develop a community roadmap that will define data needs for key questions, identify critical data gaps (e.g., underrepresented taxa) and strategies to address them, develop plans for the sustainability of existing infrastructure, and outline further development of software and infrastructure that will be needed for reproducible, FAIR and CARE-compliant research.
